title: type vs selectorText lab
blurb: Calls Element.pseudo() with 11 presets or custom strings and compares CSSPseudoElement.type against selectorText for legacy colons, whitespace normalization, escaped identifiers, null returns, and round-tripping.
question: How does CSSPseudoElement.selectorText normalize legacy colons, argument whitespace, and escaped identifiers compared with CSSPseudoElement.type, and does it round-trip back through Element.pseudo()?
result: In Chrome 153 headless, Element.prototype.pseudo() and CSSPseudoElement.type work (legacy :before normalizes to ::before; wildcard ::view-transition-group(*) and unsupported ::first-line return null), while selectorText is not exposed on CSSPseudoElement.prototype even with the blink flag. Native selectorText serialization requires Chrome 160+ or a build with CSSPseudoElementSelectorText.
testedIn: Chrome for Testing 158.0.8127.36 (Linux, headless) with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features on 2026-11-28; earlier Chrome for Testing 153.0.8010.12

friction.summary: CSSPseudoElement.type strips functional arguments, so el.pseudo(p.type) fails to re-select parameterized pseudo-elements
friction.repro: Call document.documentElement.pseudo('::view-transition-group(hero)') and pass its .type ('::view-transition-group') back to pseudo(); it returns null instead of the same object.
friction.workaround: Use p.selectorText once supported (Chrome 160+), and feature-detect via 'selectorText' in CSSPseudoElement.prototype before relying on round-tripping.
